mechaber.en:
Partners or brothers who wish to divide property that is not subject to compelled division, division of sacred books, and matters in which they do not acquire a chazakah against one another. It contains four seifim:
Partners who wish to divide an item that is not legally subject to compelled division may divide it even though by doing so they destroy its original designation. With sacred writings, meaning the twenty-four books of Tanakh written on a scroll like our Torah scroll, if they are in a single volume they may not divide them. It is degrading to the sacred books to separate them from one bound volume. Tur. Even though if one person owned them all he would be permitted to cut them apart. Hagahot Ashiri. If they are in two separate volumes, and they concern two different subjects, the rule of "buy or I will buy" does not apply; if they concern the same subject, that rule does apply. See above, siman 171, seif 13.

אין בו דינא דגוד או אגוד פי' הן שיאמר גיד את זה ואני השני ליתן האחד להשני מאי דביני ביני דיאמר השני לתרוייהו אני צריך ונלמד בו לזמנים הן שיאמר גוד אתה שניהן ותן לי חצי דמי שוויין או אני אגוד ואתן לך חלקך בדמים ויאמר לו בחד מנייהו אני אלמוד כיון דאין הא' צריך להשני וכמ"ש הטור והמחבר כל זה בסי' קע"א סעיף י"ג ע"ש ושם כתבו דיכול לו' על א' מהן גור אגוד והשני ישאר בשותפות ואם ירצו יכול לו' על שניהם גוד אגוד בזה אחר זה או לומר בפעם א' הברירה בידך לברור שניהן או איזה שתרצה או אני אעשה כן ע"ש בפרישה ובסמ"ע שכתבתי כל הדברים הללו מילתא בטעמן.
meirat_einayim.en:
Because it is degrading to the books to divide them from one bound volume. Meaning, cutting a single bound volume into two for the purpose of partition is degrading. Cutting and dividing pages or sections for one's own legitimate use is not necessarily the same degradation.
The rule of buy or sell does not apply. Meaning, neither can one say, 'You buy this one and I will take the other,' with an equalizing payment, because the other can say, 'I need both.' Nor can one say, 'You buy both and pay me half their value, or I will buy both and pay you your share,' because the other can say, 'One of them is enough for my study,' since neither book depends on the other for its use. The Tur and Mechaber explain all this in siman 171:13. There they also write that one can sometimes invoke buy-or-sell regarding one item while leaving the other in partnership. If they wish, he may present the choice regarding both sequentially, or even simultaneously say, 'The choice is yours to select both or whichever one you want, or I will do so.' See the Perishah and Sema there, where I explained the reasons.

If they divided by lot. See Radbaz, part I, siman 324. Two people jointly bought fifty cubits of cloth from a non-Jew, measured it, cut it in half, and divided the halves by lot. A defect was later found in one half that reduced its value. Radbaz rules that the division was mistaken. The lot is no stronger than a completed sale, which can be undone for a defect. Nevertheless, the lot has some effect: the partner who received the defective half may remain with that half if the other partner pays him half of the diminution in value. If the other refuses to pay the loss and instead insists on canceling the division, he may do so. They then appraise the two portions and cast lots again, with an adjustment in money so that the one who receives the defective portion is compensated. The reason the defective partner cannot insist on total cancellation where the other offers half the loss is that unlike an ordinary purchaser, who may say that he wants an entirely sound article, this partner necessarily owned half of the defect from the outset. The lot therefore can determine that he receives the entire defective portion, provided his partner equalizes the values by paying half the loss. Shaar Mishpat notes difficulties in the scope of this ruling. Radbaz's broad wording might imply that the adjustment applies whether the defect is less than one sixth or more than one sixth, which is difficult in light of siman 227:37. He therefore suggests that Radbaz may have dealt specifically with a defect amounting to exactly one sixth. Shaar Mishpat further explains that the principle is most persuasive where, before the original division, it would have been possible to divide the cloth so that each partner received half of the defect, but after the cut each resulting portion no longer admits further division. Since each was necessarily destined to bear half the defect, the lot can determine that one receives all of it with monetary equalization. If each half can still be subdivided fairly, the first division should be canceled and a proper division made. If the defect was from the outset indivisible and even with knowledge of it they would have needed a lot with monetary adjustment, Shaar Mishpat leaves open whether the original lot remains valid.
However, the Rosh wrote. See Shevut Yaakov, part III, siman 163, concerning partners who conducted a lot in the following form: whoever's name was drawn first would choose whichever share he wished, the second would then choose, and then the third. After the drawing they wished to retract. He rules that according to all opinions they may retract. Even according to Rambam and those who hold that a valid lot effects a complete acquisition, the lot must itself identify the share, like the division of Eretz Yisrael where a particular territory and a particular tribe rose together. The explanations of Rashbam, Ran, and Ri Migash likewise indicate this. A drawing that merely determines who chooses first does not itself clarify or transfer any specific share. It therefore creates no acquisition, and each party may retract.
If they divided by lot. See Responsa Radbaz, part 1, siman 324, concerning two men who purchased from a non Jew a piece of cloth fifty cubits long, measured it, cut it into two, and divided the halves by lot. A defect that reduced the value was afterward discovered in one man's share. He was asked whether the division is void. He replied that it is clear that this was a mistaken division, and the one who received the defective share may recover from his fellow for his portion of the defect. Is a lottery stronger than a completed kinyan? In a sale, if a defect is found the transaction may be rescinded. Nevertheless, he writes, the lottery was effective in one respect: each one acquired the portion that fell to him. His fellow must therefore reimburse him for half of the amount by which the defect reduced the value, if the fellow wishes. If the fellow does not wish to pay the reduction but instead wishes to annul the division, we heed him. What is done? The two portions are appraised in money and they cast lots again. Whoever receives the defective portion takes from his fellow the amount by which they valued the sound portion above it. But if the fellow wishes to give him his share of the loss caused by the defect, the division is not annulled. Although ordinarily, when one sells an item and a defect is discovered, the seller cannot say, Accept the reduction in value, because the buyer may answer, I want a complete item, as stated in siman 232, seif 4, this case is different. Here, against his will, the recipient cannot receive a completely sound item, because he must bear half of the defect in any event. Since that is so, the lottery was effective to make him the recipient of the entire defective portion, because half the defect is his in any case, while his fellow reimburses him for half of the reduction in value. This is a reasonable principle and should be followed in judgment. From the unqualified wording of the Radbaz, it appears that his ruling that the fellow reimburses half of the reduction applies even if the reduction is less than one sixth of the value, and likewise even if it is more than one sixth, the recipient must keep the portion that fell to him and his fellow merely pays half the reduction. This appears difficult in light of Shulchan Aruch below, siman 227, seif 37. I found that Shaar Mishpat at the beginning of siman 175 raises this difficulty and writes that the Radbaz must be speaking where the reduction caused by the defect is exactly one sixth, and therefore the reduction is reimbursed while the division remains in force. Shaar Mishpat further writes that the essence of the Radbaz's ruling, that the lottery was effective so that this person acquired his portion, appears to concern a case in which, before the division, the cloth could have been divided so that each would receive half of the defect, but after they divided it there is no further practicable division within either portion. In such a case the reasoning is sound: because in any event he could not have received a completely sound item, the division is effective and he bears the entire defect with reimbursement from his fellow. But if, even after the lottery, each of the two portions can still be divided, there is no basis to say that because he must accept half the defect the lottery made him accept all of it. Since they can still divide fairly, the first division is void. If the circumstances are such that from the outset the defect could not have been divided, and even had they known of it they would have needed a lottery together with monetary equalization, it requires study whether the lottery is void or not. Rashba says that if the walls of the well collapse, even if the well is rebuilt, the right of way is lost because the servitude was granted for that well and not another. This is very difficult. Sema, citing Rashba in siman 154, seif katan 25, states that as long as the underlying thing to which the servitude attached remains in existence, the servitude is not lost, such as where the wall containing a window falls and is rebuilt, or a gutter breaks and is repaired. The same should apply to the rules of siman 214 concerning an inner room and its right of passage. Even if the room collapses and is rebuilt, the passage should remain because the site to which the servitude attached still exists. I do not understand Rashba's proof from Rashbam at the end of HaMokher Et HaBayit. Rashbam says only that if a pit or cistern is destroyed and can no longer be repaired, its path right ends. That is certainly true, because the path was granted only for the pit and not for a different purpose. But if the pit is rebuilt and used again as a pit, why should the way be lost so long as the object of the servitude continues? No posek states generally that a pit or cistern loses its way permanently merely because its walls fell and were rebuilt. Perhaps Rashba's case involved an express condition when the way was acquired that the right existed only for that particular physical pit. Then, when its walls collapsed and were rebuilt, it is no longer legally the same pit. Rashba's novelty would be that ordinary debris falling into the pit and later being removed does not make it a new pit, because that is merely like removing a cover, whereas collapse of the walls and reconstruction does.

Nevertheless, beyond the strict letter of the law, one should not be overly exacting with a neighbor and relative in such a matter. See there:

He was asked about one who sold part of a house to another and stated in the deed of sale that the purchaser could use the privy, and afterward the privy collapsed and the pit was filled. Do we say that since it fell, his right is lost? He replied that at first glance this seems explicit in Shulchan Aruch at the end of siman 173 concerning a spring well, where if it collapses his established right is entirely lost. Nevertheless, he thought otherwise, because this rule is not found in the Gemara or the early authorities other than the Rashba, whose proof from the end of the chapter HaShoel, concerning lending a well, may be rejected. There it is merely a loan, and since the rule is novel, it should not be extended beyond its stated case. A privy, however, is an essential household need and use, which a person is particular to have near his residence; therefore, even if it collapses, his right should not be lost. He then saw Responsa Bach, siman 7, which writes that a privy is also comparable to a well, though he did not know the source for that ruling, and he regarded his own view as primary. He further saw Responsa Maharam Galanti, siman 67, who writes that even the Rashba spoke only where one granted the use to his fellow by way of gift or loan, but in a sale the purchaser certainly acquires the substance of the land, and one who rules otherwise is simply mistaken. This appears to him the principal ruling. See Netivot HaMishpat:

siftei_kohen.he: ואין להם זע"ז דרך כו' אע"פ שאין דרך אחר אלא זה רשב"ם בש"ס עיין בתשו' ר"ש כהן ס"ג סי' צ' וק"ט ובתשו' מהרשד"מ סי' רצ"ח וע' בסמ"ע ס"ק ז' שכתב ובדרישה הוכחתי דכאן איירי בדלא חלקו בשומא ועלוי כו' וע"ל מ"ש בשם הרא"ש בסי' קע"א וצ"ל דסמ"ע לא קאי אלשון דש"ס דאחין שחלקו אלא אלשון הטור והמחבר ודוק נ"ל ועיין מ"ש ונתן בעל הכרם לבעל השדה כו' וה"ה איפכא וכמש"ל סי' קע"ב ס"ק ה' וק"ל:
siftei_kohen.en: And they have no right of passage against one another, etc. This applies even where there is no other route, as Rashbam explains in the Gemara. See Responsa Rabbi Shlomo Kohen, volume 3, simanim 90 and 109, and Responsa Maharashdam, siman 298. See Sema, seif katan 7, who writes that in the Derishah he proved that this case concerns a division not made by appraisal and equalization. See what I wrote above in siman 171 in the name of the Rosh. The Sema must therefore be understood as commenting not on the Gemara's phrase "brothers who divided," but on the language of the Tur and Mechaber. This appears correct. Concerning the statement that the owner of the vineyard pays the owner of the field, the reverse is equally true, as I wrote above in siman 172, seif katan 5.

turei_zahav.he: (סעיף ג' אין להם דרך) כו'. מ"ש בסמ"ע סק"ז דזה מיירי בחלוקה בלא שומא ועילוי קי"ל הא כתב הרא"ש פ"ק דבתרא ומביאו הב"י סימן קע"ב ע"ד במי שחלקו בתים בשומא ועילוי דנועל לכל פתח ד' אמות דזהו בכלל העילוי ולא דמי לחלון דאינו זוכה לו בהרחקת ד"א כנגדו דהני ד"א שכנגד החלון אינם מעיקר התשמיש של הבית כ"כ וכו' ועוד התם יש לבית אורה בלאו הכי כדפי' לעיל עכ"ל הרי דפריך מחלון דאחין שחלקו אד"א של פתח שהם בשומא וכן מבואר בהדיא בגמרא פ"ק דבתרא (דף ז) ד' דמיירי בחלוקה ע"פ עילוי ושומא ומייתי עלה נהרדעי לטעמייהו דאמר ר"נ האחין שחלקו לקוחות כו' אלא דברור דאחין שחלקו מיירי ג"כ בעילוי ושומא לא מיירי כאן במאפיל לגמרי ואע"פ שכתב רבינו כאן שמסלקו לא בעי למימר מאפיל לגמרי אלא שיש רשות לכופו שיסלקנו לאפוקי מדעת הרמב"ן סימן קנ"ד דאין יכול לכפותו לסתום רק שיכול לבנות כנגדו כנלע"ד:
turei_zahav.en:
(Seif 3: They have no right of way, etc.) Sema, seif katan 7, writes that this speaks of a division made without appraisal and additional payment. This is difficult. The Rosh in the first chapter of Bava Batra, cited by Beit Yosef in siman 172, writes concerning brothers who divided houses by appraisal and equalization that each doorway receives four cubits in front of it because that was included in the appraisal. The Rosh then distinguishes this from a window, where the owner does not acquire a right requiring four cubits of open space opposite the window, because those four cubits are not so integral to the ordinary use of the house; moreover, the house has light from elsewhere. Thus the Rosh explicitly compares the rule of the window to the four cubits in front of a doorway in a division made by appraisal.
The Gemara in the first chapter of Bava Batra likewise explicitly speaks of a division by appraisal and equalization, and then cites the rule of the Nehardeans based upon Rav Nachman that brothers who divide have the status of purchasers. It is therefore clear that the case of brothers who divided here likewise concerns an appraised division.
The present ruling is not speaking of completely blocking the light. Although the Tur writes here that he may “remove it,” the meaning is not that he may totally darken the window. Rather, he may compel the other person to remove the claimed right, excluding Ramban's view in siman 154 that one cannot compel the owner to close the window but may only build opposite it. This appears correct to me.

mechaber.he: אחים שחלקו ועלה חלק א' מהם כרם ולשני שדה הלבן יש לבעל הכרם ד' אמות בשדה הלבן להפך בו מחרישתו:
mechaber.en: Brothers who shared and raised part A of whom Karmem and the other white field have the owner of the vineyard d’I will die in the white field opposite him:

baer_hetev.he: הכרם. פירוש דמיירי בדעלו אהדדי וכמו שכתב לפני זה עכ"ל הסמ"ע והיינו מעות או שטח קרקע וכ"כ הרא"ש וב"י ופשוט. ש"ך:
baer_hetev.en: The vineyard. It means that the psalmist, and as he has written before him, we have been on the ground and so forth, and so forth. “Third:

beer_hagolah.he:
מ) ל' הטור בריי' שם ד"ז ע"א
נ) סמוכות לסוף אילנות של פרדס רמב"ם בפכ"ד מה' מכירה דין י' וכ' ה"ה בהלכות ובקצת נוסחאות יש ואחד נטל כרם ובפירושי הרב אבן מיגש שדה פרדס והוא הטעם:
beer_hagolah.en:
"The column is there."
Adjacent to the ends of the orchard trees. Rambam, Hilkhot Mekhirah chapter 24, law 10. The Maggid Mishneh writes that the Halakhot and some texts read 'one took a vineyard.' Ibn Migash explains 'orchard field,' and the reason is the same.

beur_hagra.en: He has a husband. Filed to:

meirat_einayim.he: יש לבעל הכרם ד"א. פי' מיירי בדעילו אהדדי וכמ"ש לפני זה ע"ש:
meirat_einayim.en: The owner of the vineyard has four cubits. Meaning that the case involves appraisal and an equalizing payment, as I wrote immediately above.

netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.he: יש לבעל הכרם מיירי בשומא ועילוי:
netivot_hamishpat_hidushim.en: The owner of the vineyard is intoxicated:

siftei_kohen.he: יש לבעל הכרם ד"א פי' מיירי בדעלו אהדדי וכמ"ש לפני זה עכ"ל סמ"ע והיינו מעות או שטח קרקע וכ"כ הרא"ש וב"י ופשוט:
siftei_kohen.en: The owner of the vineyard has four cubits. The case is one where they made an appraisal and equalization between themselves, as explained immediately above. This is the Sema's explanation. The equalization may be in money or by adding an area of land. The Rosh and Beit Yosef write likewise. This is straightforward.
